atlas-ie.0001: In 2025 the employment rate of Irish people aged 20 to 34 with a tertiary degree was 91.6% (92.0% for those who left education within the last three years); the job vacancy rate was 1.3% in the last quarter of 2025.
atlas-ie.0002: Deloitte Ireland’s 2027 Future Leaders Academy (audit and assurance) closes at 17:00 on 21 October 2026, and PwC Ireland’s summer internship applications open on 2 December 2026 and close on 29 January 2027.
atlas-ie.0003: Most Irish graduate employers set no specific deadline and take applications for most of the year; the Gradireland Graduate Careers Fair is held in October (6 October 2026, RDS Dublin) and university fairs run from October to February.
atlas-ie.0004: An English-speaking EU market built on multinationals: IDA-backed foreign companies employ about 312,000 people, around one job in nine, and Dublin holds two thirds of Ireland’s jobs in information and communication and in finance, with fund administration and aircraft leasing on top. Cork is the second centre for both. Non-EU master’s graduates can search for work for up to two years.
atlas-ie.0009: Galway and Limerick are not mapped as hubs: IDA Ireland’s annual report gives only regional jobs (West 32,562, Mid-West 28,125), and no city-level employer or sector source could be read; the regional pages of IDA Ireland could not be read.
atlas-ie.0010: All Irish immigration, visa, residence permit and salary rules are consolidated from primary sources in visas_immigration/ireland/ireland_visas_immigration_guide.md.
atlas-ie.0011: Dublin’s ratings rest on Eurostat’s 2021 metropolitan employment counts and the funds-industry figures, not on a Dublin figure for each role family; software, data and AI are not rated.
atlas-ie.0012: Dublin GDP is Eurostat’s 2021 figure and is inflated by multinationals’ profits booked in Ireland; pay and rent are county figures (County Dublin, County Cork), which reach beyond the cities.
atlas-ie.0013: Employers are named from their own graduate-programme pages; no headcount for any of them in Dublin was read, and the CRO company register could not be queried.
atlas-ie.0014: Cork’s rating rests on Eurostat’s 2021 count (second in Ireland for both families); no named Cork employer in finance or IT was read.
atlas-ie.0017: European headquarters of US tech firms, fund administration and aircraft leasing
atlas-ie.0018: graduate programmes; new Dublin headquarters at Harcourt Square
atlas-ie.0020: 2026 graduate programme, with Tax and Law and Technology routes
atlas-ie.0021: annual graduate programme; the 2028 intake is open for registration of interest
atlas-ie.0026: Ireland’s second city for finance and for information-and-communication jobs
atlas-ie.0027: Irish facility and European telephone-support team based in Cork
atlas-ie.0028: IDA-backed multinationals employed 312,468 people in 2025, about 11% of national employment, across more than 1,800 operations; 54% of these jobs are outside Dublin.
atlas-ie.0029: Dublin hosts the European headquarters of US tech firms, fund administration and aircraft leasing.
atlas-ie.0030: English is the working language: only 2.4–2.8% of Irish job postings say English is not required.
atlas-ie.0031: Eurostat counts 339,530 people in work in the Cork metropolitan region in 2021: 16,660 in information and communication (second in Ireland, after Dublin) and 8,150 in finance and insurance (second in Ireland, after Dublin). The region’s GDP was €115.7 billion in 2021.
atlas-ie.0032: Eurostat counts 1,073,000 people in work in the Dublin metropolitan region in 2021: 97,700 in information and communication, 65% of Ireland’s 149,400 and the most of any Irish region, and 80,700 in finance and insurance, 68% of the national 118,800.
atlas-ie.0033: Among the 152 European metropolitan regions with 2021 figures, Dublin ranks tenth by jobs in information and communication (97,700) and fourth by jobs in finance and insurance (80,700), behind only Paris, Warsaw and Milan; London, Berlin, Frankfurt and Madrid report no figure for that year.
atlas-ie.0034: Dublin is 30th in the world in the Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) and 10th among Western European centres; Cork is not ranked among the ones listed.
atlas-ie.0035: Irish Funds says the funds and asset-management industry directly employed 19,519 people in Ireland in 2023, according to an Indecon report it commissioned, with over 37,500 jobs in total once indirect effects are counted.
atlas-ie.0036: The CSO counts 3,005 people employed in aircraft leasing in Ireland in 2024, at average earnings of €206,324 a year.
atlas-ie.0037: IDA-supported companies employed 142,501 people in the Dublin region in 2025 and 53,535 in the South-West (Cork and Kerry), 32,562 in the West, 28,125 in the Mid-West and 169,967 outside Dublin in all; information and communication accounted for 112,300 of the 312,468 jobs and business, financial and other services for 61,155.
atlas-ie.0038: One year after graduating, the median weekly earnings of the 2022 cohort were €650 for master’s graduates in business, administration and law and €855 for those in information and communication technologies (€570 and €770 for bachelor’s graduates); 84% of the cohort were in substantial employment and the all-graduate median was €625 a week.
atlas-ie.0039: Ireland’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 5.0% in September 2026, and 12.5% for 15-to-24-year-olds.
atlas-ie.0040: KPMG Ireland runs graduate programmes and says its new Dublin headquarters, Harcourt Square, opens in 2026.
atlas-ie.0041: Deloitte Ireland runs a graduate programme, its Future Leaders Academy, with intakes it says are always 50/50 by gender.
atlas-ie.0042: EY Ireland lists a 2026 Graduate Programme, with routes including Tax and Law and Technology.
atlas-ie.0043: Bank of Ireland says its 2027 Graduate Programme is closed for applications and invites candidates to register interest in the 2028 programme.
atlas-ie.0044: Apple’s job-creation page shows Cork as the base of its Irish facility, which it says builds iMac for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and of a team giving telephone support to customers across Europe.
atlas-ie.0045: Ireland hires graduates mostly through structured programmes at the Big Four, banks and the multinationals based in Dublin, and through work placements built into Irish degrees. Unlike the UK, most Irish employers have no fixed deadline and take applications for most of the year.
atlas-ie.0046: The professional-services firms are the exception: Deloitte’s 2027 audit programme closes at 17:00 on 21 October 2026, and its page says you can apply to only one graduate programme.
atlas-ie.0047: The Big Four, Bank of Ireland, AIB and Citi run graduate intakes in Dublin, with online tests and assessment days.
atlas-ie.0048: Gradireland’s survey of graduate employers found 46% use a telephone interview, 42% online ability or technical tests, 39% online psychometric tests and 37% video interviews; 54% look for a 2:1 or better.
atlas-ie.0049: KPMG Ireland offers a Chartered Accountant (ACA) route and a STEM and non-ACA route, Deloitte’s Future Leaders Academy takes any discipline with a 2.1, and EY takes any degree and discipline with a 2:1.
atlas-ie.0051: Many Irish degrees include a paid placement of several months, which employers use as a trial before the graduate offer.
atlas-ie.0052: PwC Ireland’s summer internship applications open on 2 December 2026 and close on 29 January 2027, and State Street runs a 12-month in-person internship in Dublin.
atlas-ie.0053: Direct applications and referrals at multinationals
atlas-ie.0054: Google, Meta, Microsoft, Apple, Pfizer and the payment firms hire graduates in Dublin, often in multilingual operations and sales roles that welcome other European languages.
atlas-ie.0055: Experienced hires apply through the same online portals and recruiters; a Critical Skills permit lets a non-EU hire with an offer of at least €40,904 start without a labour-market test.
atlas-ie.0057: The Gradireland Graduate Careers Fair took place on 6 October 2026 at the RDS in Dublin with over 80 employers; first-term fairs and presentations still happen, but are now used mainly to engage finalists, not to set closing dates.
atlas-ie.0058: University fairs follow: the Trinity engineering fair and UCC Recruitment Festival on 8 October, ATU Galway on 20 October, and the University of Limerick spring fair in late January and February.
atlas-ie.0060: publicjobs.ie is the public service recruitment site, with job search, alerts and guidance on applications, tests and interviews; its page lists a news item on graduate opportunities in the civil service.
atlas-ie.0061: Apprenticeships now reach professional work: 87 programmes in 17 sectors, 30,536 apprentices and 10,191 companies by mid-2026, including a two-year accounting technician and a three-year insurance practitioner route that ends in a BA (Hons).
atlas-ie.0062: Just over 80% of the class of 2024 were in work nine months after graduating; in the 2026 employer survey, 66% planned to hire graduates as planned and a further 24% were hiring more cautiously.
atlas-ie.0063: Dublin depends on a few multinationals, so a round of tech lay-offs hits graduate hiring quickly.
atlas-ie.0064: The old model of campaigns with deadlines before Christmas is no longer the reality: gradireland says the majority of companies in Ireland do not have a specific deadline, and EY says that unless a closing date is stated, applications close once the roles are filled.
atlas-ie.0065: The vacancy rate is low at 1.3% in the last quarter of 2025 (2.5% in professional, scientific and technical activities), so competition for graduate places is stiff.
atlas-ie.0066: Employers say they look for core competencies and employability skills (65%) and a 2:1 or better (54%); the Big Four pages read name no target universities and accept any discipline.
